description: Replica Amazon product detail page (Logitech MX Master 3S mouse) with deliberately injected dark patterns and counterexamples. Used to measure the identification prompt's true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative rates.
page_url_when_served: http://localhost:8000/amazon-product-page.html (or any http:// host; the extension rejects file:// URLs)

user_primary_intent_acceptable: buy the Logitech MX Master 3S wireless mouse
add this mouse to cart / complete this purchase
expected_page_evaluation.scoring_note: Mark page_evaluation correct if page_type == 'product_detail' AND user_primary_intent is a reasonable paraphrase of 'buy this mouse'. If the model says the intent is something vague ('shopping', 'browsing') or wrong ('read reviews', 'cancel a subscription'), mark it incorrect — every downstream harm test depends on this.

dark_patterns.element: Modal overlay promoting a Ninja Air Fryer ('An Irresistible Offer Just For You!')
dark_patterns.why: Promotional content unrelated to the user's task (buying a mouse); the only dismiss control is a near-invisible '×' (opacity 0.12, white text, parked in the page corner away from the modal) while the modal's 'Add to Cart — $89.99' CTA is full-width and prominent. Unrelated promotion + degraded dismiss path.

dark_patterns.element: 'See additional fees for this item' collapsed <details> near the price
dark_patterns.why: Mandatory, unavoidable fees ($12.99 handling + $8.50 packaging = $21.49, ~21% over the headline $99.99) are concealed inside a collapsed, low-contrast disclosure. A user who clicks Add to Cart without expanding it never sees the true total ($121.48). Decision-critical cost hidden behind a non-default reveal at the moment of commitment.

dark_patterns.element: Urgency/scarcity badges: '17 people are viewing this right now', 'Only 2 left in stock — order soon!', 'Bought 340+ times in the past month'
dark_patterns.why: Unverifiable popularity/scarcity claims with no source or methodology, used to pressure an immediate purchase. The viewer count, stock count, and purchase count cannot be audited by the user.

dark_patterns.element: Pre-checked checkbox 'Email me about deals and new releases on Logitech products' inside the buy box
dark_patterns.why: Opts the user into marketing email by default; benefits Amazon, not the user; embedded in a focused checkout flow where it's easy to miss; reverses what a user explicitly asked would choose.

dark_patterns.element: A fake 'ADD TO CART' button injected above the real one, styled like Amazon's yellow CTA but larger, with a tiny low-contrast 'Advertisement' label
dark_patterns.why: Mimics Amazon's native primary CTA but the onclick/href navigates to an external affiliate offer (deals.shopnow-partner.example), not to this product's cart. Clicking does NOT do what the label promises — destination mismatch + impersonation.

dark_patterns.element: 'Protect your purchase' section: large bright pill button 'Add 3-Year Protection — $19.99' vs a tiny, gray, no-underline, thin-weight 'no thanks' link
dark_patterns.why: The user came to buy a mouse; the visually dominant CTA pushes a paid add-on that benefits Amazon, and the decline option matching the user's intent is visually buried (smallest font, low-contrast gray, no underline). Prominence misaligned with user intent.

dark_patterns.element: Notification permission banner with two equally-styled buttons: 'I want no notifications' and 'I do not want no notifications'
dark_patterns.why: Double-negative labels. A hurried user reads 'I do not want no notifications' as 'I don't want notifications' and clicks it — but it OPTS THEM IN. The semantic inversion is in the button label itself.

dark_patterns.element: Prime trial card; decline link reads 'No thanks, I'd rather pay full price and wait longer for my order'
dark_patterns.why: The decline option's LABEL shames the user for choosing the free path, framing it as a self-inflicted loss ('pay full price and wait longer'). The manipulation is in the wording of the decline control.

counterexamples.element: 'Hello, sign in / Account & Lists' link in the top nav
counterexamples.why_not: A plain navigation link. Nothing on this page is blocked behind signing in; the user can view the product, price, reviews, and add to cart without an account. No coercion.

counterexamples.element: '4.6 out of 5 · 12,453 ratings' linking to the on-page reviews
counterexamples.why_not: A genuine review aggregate from a disclosed, auditable source — it links directly to the underlying reviews (visible in the #reviews section, with verified-purchase tags). It informs rather than pressures; no urgency framing.

counterexamples.element: Delivery options with 'Standard Shipping — FREE' radio pre-selected
counterexamples.why_not: A radio is pre-selected, but it's the cheapest, user-favoring option — a sensible default. Nothing is being extracted from the user (no paid add-on, no consent, no recurring charge).

counterexamples.element: 'Product details' collapsed <details> accordion (connectivity, weight, dimensions, ASIN)
counterexamples.why_not: The collapsed content is general, non-decision-critical reference info (specs), not material costs or terms. The price and shipping are already visible above. Normal progressive disclosure.

counterexamples.element: The real yellow 'Add to Cart' button in the buy box (#addToCart_feature_div)
counterexamples.why_not: A prominent yellow CTA — same visual weight asymmetry vs surrounding text as the disguised fake — but it does exactly what its label promises: adds THIS product to the cart on THIS site. Prominence matches the user's intent on a product page. Visual prominence alone is never sufficient evidence.

counterexamples.element: The real orange 'Buy Now' button in the buy box
counterexamples.why_not: Legitimate primary action on a product page; the destination is the purchase flow for this product. Colored prominent CTA != dark pattern.

counterexamples.element: '♡ Add to List' small low-contrast text link below the buy buttons
counterexamples.why_not: Visual asymmetry vs the big CTAs exists, but this is a legitimate secondary affordance (wishlist), not a primary option being suppressed against the user's interest.

counterexamples.element: 'Sponsored — products related to this item' carousel with a clear 'Sponsored' header
counterexamples.why_not: These are ads, but honestly labeled with a prominent 'Sponsored' header and visually distinct from organic content — no impersonation of native primary actions. Having labeled ads on a page is not a dark pattern.

scoring.true_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `dark_patterns` gt_id (by css_selector / html_evidence overlap) AND whose dark_pattern_type is in that entry's `accepts_types`.
scoring.false_negative: A `dark_patterns` gt_id has no matching entry in the model output.
scoring.false_positive: Model output contains an entry whose target element matches a `counterexamples` gt_id, OR an entry whose target element matches no gt_id at all.
scoring.wrong_type: Model flags the right element (a `dark_patterns` gt_id) but with a dark_pattern_type NOT in `accepts_types`. Count separately from TP/FP — it found something real but mislabeled it.
scoring.page_eval: Separately, score expected_page_evaluation as correct/incorrect per its scoring_note.
headline_metrics: recall = TP / (TP + FN)   [TP + FN = 8, the count of injected dark patterns]
false_positive_rate = FP / (number of counterexamples + extraneous flags)  — this is the metric the recent prompt rewrite targets

Note: maxItems is 3 in the schema, so the model can report at most 3 patterns per run. Recall is bounded by 3/8 in a single pass — run the page multiple times, or accept that 'top 3' coverage is the realistic ceiling. Track WHICH 3 it picks and whether they are all real.
